questions.explanation: In the RADIUS login process, the user's credentials go to the access device, which sends an Access-Request to the RADIUS server and acts on the Access-Accept, Access-Reject, or Access-Challenge. The access device (switch or AP) is the RADIUS client, not the user's endpoint.
questions.discriminator_tested: The access device is the RADIUS client.

questions.stem: Which password approach BEST resists guessing?

options.text: A 10-character password mixing four character types
options.rationale: Complexity helps, but length adds more strength.

options.text: An 8-character password changed monthly
options.rationale: Frequent changes don't make a short password hard to guess.

options.text: A random 20-character passphrase of words
options.rationale: Correct: length multiplies the search space.

options.text: A dictionary word with a number and symbol added
options.rationale: Predictable substitutions are in every cracking list.

questions.explanation: Longer passwords with mixed character types resist guessing, and length adds more strength than complexity alone: each extra character multiplies the search space, while predictable substitutions add little.
questions.discriminator_tested: Length adds more strength than complexity alone.

questions.stem: An attacker deliberately enters wrong passwords against each executive's account. With a lockout policy of five attempts, what is the MOST likely effect?

options.text: The lockout policy is disabled automatically
options.rationale: Policies don't switch themselves off.

options.text: The attacker's guessing is stopped after five tries
options.rationale: True, but the attacker wasn't trying to guess.

options.text: The executives are locked out, denying them service
options.rationale: Correct: the lockout itself becomes the attack.

options.text: The attacker learns the executives' passwords
options.rationale: Wrong guesses reveal nothing.

questions.explanation: Password lockout locks an account after a set number of failed attempts. It counters online brute force but can itself be abused to lock out legitimate users.
questions.discriminator_tested: Lockout counters brute force but can be abused to lock out users.

questions.stem: A user's PC on port Gi1/0/9 gets no network access. The switch shows the status below. What BEST explains it?

Interface:   Gi1/0/9
Status:      Unauthorized
Allowed:     EAPOL only
Last event:  EAP timeout (no supplicant response)

options.text: The port is blocking the PC's traffic
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why.

options.text: The switch port is administratively shut down
options.rationale: A shut port wouldn't show EAPOL activity.

options.text: The port passes only EAPOL until the PC authenticates
options.rationale: Correct: the PC never answered, so the port stays blocked.

options.text: The PC was given a 169.254 address by the switch
options.rationale: Switches don't assign APIPA addresses.

questions.stem: In an 802.1X deployment, which component decides whether the user is allowed on, and which enforces that decision at the port?

options.rationale: Correct: authentication server decides, authenticator enforces.

questions.discriminator_tested: The authenticator enforces; the server decides.

questions.stem: Which order BEST describes the NAC process for a device joining the network?

options.text: Connect, apply policy access, identify and assess
options.rationale: Access is set before anything is known about the device.

options.rationale: The device must connect before it can be assessed.

options.text: Connect, identify and assess, apply policy access
options.rationale: Correct: policy can only act on what was learned.

options.text: Apply policy access, connect, identify and assess
options.rationale: Policy can't apply to a device that hasn't connected.

questions.explanation: In the NAC process, a device connects, is identified and assessed, and then policy sets its access level: full, restricted, quarantine, or deny. The outcome need not be all-or-nothing.
questions.discriminator_tested: NAC outcome is policy-driven and need not be all-or-nothing.

MAC 00:1b:a9:3e:7c:11     OUI: Brother Industries
DHCP option 55: 1,3,6,15,44,47     hostname: BRN001BA93E7C11

options.text: 802.1X authentication
options.rationale: The device can't run a supplicant.

options.text: Guest isolation
options.rationale: Isolation is a placement decision, not identification.

options.text: Posture assessment
options.rationale: Posture checks health such as patches and antivirus, not device type.

options.text: Profiling
options.rationale: Correct: it worked out what the device is from observed attributes.

questions.explanation: Profiling identifies what a device is (its type or class) from observed attributes such as MAC vendor, DHCP options, and open ports. It suits devices that can't run a supplicant, such as printers and IoT devices.
questions.discriminator_tested: Profiling identifies device type; suits devices without a supplicant.

questions.stem: Profiling, posture assessment, and 802.1X authentication each answer a different question about a device. Which question does posture assessment answer?

options.text: Who is the user or device?
options.rationale: That is authentication.

options.text: Which VLAN did DHCP assign it?
options.rationale: DHCP doesn't assign VLANs.

options.text: What kind of device is it?
options.rationale: That is profiling.

options.text: Is the device healthy and compliant?
options.rationale: Correct: patches, antivirus, configuration.

questions.explanation: Posture assessment checks a device's health and compliance (patches, antivirus, configuration). It answers health, while authentication answers identity and profiling answers type.
questions.discriminator_tested: Health vs identity vs type.

questions.stem: A hospital will let staff use personal phones for email and the scheduling app. Which two controls BEST address the risk? (Choose two.)

options.text: Training staff on phishing
options.rationale: Useful, but it doesn't address unmanaged devices on the network.

options.text: Posture checks before granting access
options.rationale: Correct: unmanaged devices must meet a health baseline.

options.text: Allowing personal devices on the clinical VLAN
options.rationale: The opposite of segmentation.

options.text: A segment that limits personal devices to approved apps
options.rationale: Correct: segmentation keeps them away from clinical systems.

options.text: A captive portal that encrypts their Wi-Fi traffic
options.rationale: A portal is a gate, not encryption.

questions.explanation: BYOD means personally owned devices accessing organizational resources. Because they are unmanaged and varied, BYOD needs NAC, posture checks, and segmentation.
questions.discriminator_tested: BYOD is unmanaged and varied: needs NAC, posture, segmentation.

questions.stem: A hotel offers Wi-Fi to conference attendees. Which design BEST meets the goal of guest network isolation?

options.text: A captive portal on the staff network
options.rationale: A portal gates entry but doesn't isolate guests.

options.text: The staff network with a separate password
options.rationale: A different password still puts guests on the staff network.

options.text: WPA3 on the staff network to stop snooping
options.rationale: Encryption doesn't separate guests from internal systems.

options.text: A separate segment with internet-only access
options.rationale: Correct: guests can't reach internal resources.

questions.explanation: Guest network isolation places guests on a separate segment with internet-only access, isolated from internal resources.
questions.discriminator_tested: Guest isolation = separate segment, internet-only.

questions.stem: A cafe's Wi-Fi shows a terms page before allowing internet access. A customer assumes the page means their traffic is now encrypted. What BEST describes the page?

options.text: A WPA3 handshake shown as a web page
options.rationale: Wi-Fi encryption happens before any web page.

options.text: A gate for access, not encryption of traffic
options.rationale: Correct: it controls entry; the network may still be open.

options.text: A VPN that starts when terms are accepted
options.rationale: Accepting terms doesn't start a VPN.

options.text: A login page that records who accepted the terms
options.rationale: Often true, but it doesn't address the encryption assumption.

questions.explanation: A captive portal intercepts a new user's first request and requires login or acceptance before granting access. It is a gate for guest and BYOD onboarding, not encryption of wireless traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: Captive portal is a gate, not encryption.

questions.stem: Which change BEST ensures that the local account below has its password stored as a hash?

options.text: Enable 'service password-encryption'
options.rationale: Hides it from casual view, but type 7 encoding is weak and reversible.

options.text: Raise the account to privilege 15
options.rationale: Privilege level has nothing to do with how the password is stored.

options.text: Add 'login local' to the VTY lines
options.rationale: That applies local accounts to logins; it doesn't change storage.

options.text: Recreate it with 'secret' instead of 'password'
options.rationale: Correct: 'secret' stores a one-way hash.

questions.explanation: Local authentication stores accounts on the device. 'secret' stores a one-way hash; 'password' stores the text, and 'service password-encryption' applies only weak, reversible type 7 encoding.
questions.discriminator_tested: 'secret' is hashed; 'password' is not.

questions.stem: Which two of these records are produced by the accounting part of the iAAA model? (Choose two.)

options.text: TACACS+: 'configure terminal' denied for jtan
options.rationale: That is an authorization decision.

options.text: Login prompt: user typed 'cwong'
options.rationale: Claiming an identity is identification.

options.text: VPN: asmith's session lasted 2 h 11 min, 340 MB
options.rationale: Correct: session data is accounting.

options.text: Router1: jtan ran 'reload' at 02:14
options.rationale: Correct: a record of what was done and when.

options.text: RADIUS: Access-Reject for bjones
options.rationale: That is an authentication result.

questions.explanation: The iAAA model is identification, authentication, authorization, and accounting. Accounting records who did what and when, such as commands and session data.
questions.discriminator_tested: Accounting = what did you do.

questions.stem: A user signs in with a password and then approves a push prompt on their registered phone. Which factor categories were used?

options.text: Something you know, used twice
options.rationale: Approving the push proves possession of the phone, not knowledge.

options.text: Something you are and somewhere you are
options.rationale: Neither a biometric nor location was checked.

options.text: Something known plus something held
options.rationale: Correct: the password is knowledge; the registered phone is possession.

options.text: Something you have and something you are
options.rationale: No biometric was used.

questions.explanation: Authentication verifies a claimed identity using factors: something you know (the password), have (the registered phone), or are (biometrics). Approving the push proves possession of the phone.
questions.discriminator_tested: Factor categories: know, have, are.

questions.stem: A website asks for a password and then for the user's mother's maiden name, and calls this 'two-factor authentication'. Which answer is BEST?

options.text: Not MFA; the second answer is easy to research
options.rationale: True, but the reason it isn't MFA is the shared category.

options.text: It is MFA; the question is something the user is
options.rationale: A remembered fact is knowledge, not inherence.

options.text: It is MFA; there are two separate checks
options.rationale: Two checks aren't enough; they must be different categories.

options.text: Not MFA; both are things the user knows
options.rationale: Correct: two checks from one category.

questions.explanation: MFA requires two or more different factor categories. A password plus a security question are both knowledge, so this is single-factor authentication done twice.
questions.discriminator_tested: Factors must come from different categories.

questions.stem: An attacker convinces a mobile carrier to move a victim's phone number to a new SIM card. Which MFA method does this MOST directly defeat?

options.text: Codes from an authenticator app
options.rationale: App codes are generated on the device, not delivered to the number.

options.text: A hardware token's rotating code
options.rationale: The token works without a phone number.

options.text: A fingerprint reader on the laptop
options.rationale: Moving a phone number has no effect on a biometric.

options.text: One-time codes sent by SMS
options.rationale: Correct: the codes now arrive on the attacker's SIM.

questions.explanation: MFA methods include email, SMS, voice calls, and time-based hardware or software tokens. Time-based tokens are generally stronger, because SMS, voice, and email codes can be intercepted or redirected.
questions.discriminator_tested: SMS/voice/email codes can be intercepted or redirected.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes authorization from authentication?

options.text: It records what the user did afterward
options.rationale: That is accounting.

options.text: It decides what a verified user may do
options.rationale: Correct: permissions, not identity.

options.text: It happens after the user has logged in
options.rationale: True of the order, but not what it does.

options.text: It checks the user's password or token
options.rationale: That is authentication.

questions.explanation: Authorization determines what an authenticated user may access or do, and it happens after authentication.
questions.discriminator_tested: Authorization = what may you do; after authentication.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes how IAM relates to AAA?

options.text: They are two names for the same thing
options.rationale: IAM covers the whole identity lifecycle, not just AAA.

options.text: IAM is the overall program; AAA is one mechanism in it
options.rationale: Correct: IAM is the umbrella.

options.text: AAA is the overall program; IAM is one part of it
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: Both control access to systems
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't describe how they relate.

questions.explanation: Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the processes and tools that manage identities and their access across their lifecycle. It is the umbrella program; AAA is one mechanism inside it.
questions.discriminator_tested: IAM is the umbrella; AAA is one mechanism inside it.

questions.stem: Malware on a developer's laptop encrypted the company's production database server. The developer needed read access to one test database and nothing more. What BEST explains why the damage was so large?

options.text: The developer's password was too short
options.rationale: The malware ran under the developer's logged-in account; no password was guessed.

options.text: The account had excess access
options.rationale: Correct: the malware could do whatever the developer's account could.

options.text: The production server had no recent backups
options.rationale: That affects recovery, not how much was damaged.

options.text: The malware wasn't detected by antivirus
options.rationale: Detection failed, but the reach came from the account's access.

questions.explanation: Least privilege grants only the access needed to do the job. It limits the damage from mistakes, malware, and insiders: had the account held only read access to the test database, the malware could have reached only that.
questions.discriminator_tested: Least privilege limits damage from malware.

questions.stem: A company has 3,000 staff in 25 job functions, and IT spends days editing individual users' permissions. Which access model BEST reduces this work?

options.text: Per-user permissions managed by a script
options.rationale: Faster, but still per-individual assignment.

options.text: Discretionary access set by file owners
options.rationale: Spreads the work around instead of reducing it.

options.text: RBAC, assigning permissions to job roles
options.rationale: Correct: change 25 roles instead of 3,000 users.

options.text: One shared admin account per department
options.rationale: Removes accountability and grants too much.

questions.explanation: In RBAC, permissions attach to roles and users get access through their role, not through per-individual assignment.
questions.discriminator_tested: RBAC is role-based, not per-individual.

questions.stem: A core link went down at 02:14. The AAA server holds the record below. What does it BEST establish?

02:14:07 router1 jtan tty1 10.1.9.40 start  task_id=811

02:14:40 router1 jtan cmd="shutdown"
02:15:02 router1 jtan stop   task_id=811 elapsed=55s

options.text: jtan's account was locked after the change
options.rationale: Nothing in the record shows a lockout.

options.text: jtan shut down Gi0/1 at 02:14:40
options.rationale: Correct: the accounting trail ties the command to the user and time.

options.text: jtan was logged in to router1 at the time
options.rationale: True, but the record shows much more: the exact command.

options.text: The link failed because of a hardware fault
options.rationale: The record shows a deliberate shutdown command.

questions.explanation: Accounting records who did what and when (logins, commands, session data). It is the after-the-fact audit trail that enables traceability.
questions.discriminator_tested: Accounting enables traceability.

questions.stem: An analyst captures the packet below. What does it show about how RADIUS protects the request?

UDP 10.1.1.2:51515 -> 10.1.9.30:1812  Access-Request
  User-Name          = "asmith"
  User-Password      = <hidden>
  NAS-IP-Address     = 10.1.1.2
  Called-Station-Id  = "AP-2F:CorpNet"

options.rationale: That is TACACS+; here the other attributes are readable.

options.text: Just the password is hidden; the rest is readable
options.rationale: Correct: RADIUS hides only the password attribute.

options.text: Nothing is hidden; RADIUS is cleartext
options.rationale: The password attribute is hidden.

options.text: The request is protected by TLS on port 1812
options.rationale: Standard RADIUS runs over plain UDP, not TLS.

questions.discriminator_tested: RADIUS encrypts only the password.

questions.stem: A company wants each command its network administrators type on 500 routers checked against their role and logged. Which AAA protocol BEST fits?

options.text: Local accounts
options.rationale: Not centralized across 500 routers.

options.text: SNMPv3
options.rationale: A management protocol, not AAA.

options.text: RADIUS
options.rationale: Combines authentication and authorization; suited to network access, not per-command control.

options.text: TACACS+
options.rationale: Correct: separate authorization allows per-command control.

questions.explanation: TACACS+ is Cisco-originated AAA over TCP 49 that encrypts the entire payload and separates authentication, authorization, and accounting. That separation makes it typical for device administration.
questions.discriminator_tested: TACACS+ separates the three As; typical for device administration.

questions.stem: Administrators report that their TACACS+ accounts don't work on the router below, although local accounts do. What is the MOST likely cause?
questions.exhibit:
aaa new-model

aaa authentication login VTY-LOGIN group tacacs+ local

options.text: TACACS+ needs UDP 1812 opened on the firewall
options.rationale: TACACS+ uses TCP 49; 1812 is RADIUS.

options.text: The VTY lines are using local authentication

questions.discriminator_tested: Method lists must be applied to lines.

questions.stem: A RADIUS server logs the exchange below. What does the Access-Challenge BEST indicate?

10.1.9.30 -> 10.1.1.2   Access-Challenge  (enter one-time code)
10.1.1.2  -> 10.1.9.30  Access-Request    User-Name=asmith (with code)

options.text: The user's login was rejected outright

questions.discriminator_tested: Accept, Reject, or Challenge; the access device is the RADIUS client.

questions.stem: Policy requires 8 characters including uppercase, lowercase, a number, and a symbol, yet most passwords look like 'Spring26!'. Which change BEST improves resistance to guessing?

options.rationale: Correct: length adds far more strength than extra symbols.

options.rationale: More complexity helps a little, but 'Spring26!!' is still easy.

options.text: Force a password change each month
options.rationale: Frequent changes push people toward predictable patterns.

questions.explanation: Longer passwords with mixed character types resist guessing, and length adds more strength than complexity alone.
questions.discriminator_tested: Length adds more strength than complexity alone.

questions.stem: An attacker tries thousands of passwords against one VPN account. Which control MOST directly stops this?

options.text: Require longer passwords
options.rationale: Makes guessing slower, but the attempts continue.

options.text: Lock it after a few failed attempts
options.rationale: Correct: caps the number of online guesses.

options.text: Encrypt the VPN with a stronger cipher
options.rationale: Encryption doesn't limit login attempts.

options.text: Block passwords on breach lists

questions.explanation: Password lockout locks an account after a set number of failed attempts, which counters online brute force. It can itself be abused to lock out legitimate users.
questions.discriminator_tested: Lockout counters online brute force.

questions.stem: Visitors keep plugging laptops into empty conference-room wall jacks and getting full network access. Which control BEST stops this?

options.text: Shutting down unused wall jacks
options.rationale: Helps, but a visitor can unplug a desk phone or PC and use that jack.

options.text: WPA3 on the company's Wi-Fi
options.rationale: The visitors are on wired ports.

options.text: 802.1X port authentication
options.rationale: Correct: the port passes nothing but authentication traffic until the device proves itself.

options.text: A captive portal on the wired network
options.rationale: A portal can be accepted by anyone; it isn't port authentication.

questions.explanation: 802.1X is port-based access control: a port passes only authentication traffic until the device authenticates, so an unknown laptop gets nothing.
questions.discriminator_tested: 802.1X: the port stays blocked until success.

questions.stem: Which two pairings of 802.1X role and device are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Authentication server: the access switch
options.rationale: The authentication server is RADIUS.

questions.discriminator_tested: Supplicant, authenticator, authentication server.

questions.stem: A laptop passes identity checks but fails posture because its antivirus is out of date. Under a typical NAC policy, what happens next?

options.rationale: Correct: a restricted, fix-and-retry outcome.

questions.explanation: In the NAC process, a device connects, is identified and assessed, and policy sets its access level: full, restricted, quarantine, or deny. The outcome is policy-driven and need not be all-or-nothing.
questions.discriminator_tested: NAC outcome need not be all-or-nothing.

questions.stem: A hospital has hundreds of infusion pumps and badge readers that can't run 802.1X software. Which NAC capability BEST lets it place them in the right segment automatically?

options.text: Posture assessment
options.rationale: Posture checks health, and these devices can't run an agent.

options.text: Device profiling
options.rationale: Correct: it identifies the device type from observed attributes.

options.text: SMS-based MFA
options.rationale: Devices don't receive text messages.

questions.explanation: Profiling identifies what a device is (its type or class) from observed attributes. It suits devices that can't run a supplicant, such as printers, medical equipment, and IoT.
questions.discriminator_tested: Profiling suits devices that can't run a supplicant.

questions.stem: Which two checks are part of posture assessment? (Choose two.)

options.text: The user's password is correct

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes the risk of BYOD from that of company-owned laptops?

options.text: The devices are often newer models

options.rationale: Personal devices use the same bands.

questions.discriminator_tested: BYOD devices are unmanaged and varied.

questions.stem: A conference venue wants attendees to accept terms and enter an event code before using its Wi-Fi. Which feature BEST fits?

options.text: Device profiling
options.rationale: Profiling identifies device types; it doesn't interact with users.

options.text: A captive portal
options.rationale: Correct: a web gate for guest onboarding.

options.text: WPA3-Personal
options.rationale: A shared passphrase can't show terms or collect a code.

options.text: 802.1X with RADIUS
options.rationale: Possible, but heavy for one-day guests who need individual accounts.

questions.explanation: A captive portal intercepts a new user's first request and requires login or acceptance before granting access. It is a gate for guest and BYOD onboarding, not encryption.
questions.discriminator_tested: Captive portal is a gate for guest onboarding.
